title: Why Predators Thrive in Rule-Heavy Systems
author: Foster Chance
summary: Foster Chance argues that rule-heavy organizations are not safer than others -- they are often actively more dangerous, because sophisticated manipulators weaponize procedural compliance as cover for ethical violations. The central insight, grounded in Dark Triad research, is that narcissistic and Machiavellian individuals are disproportionately drawn to status-and-influence environments and become expert at exploiting the institutional confusion between procedural compliance and ethical behavior. Chance illustrates the mechanism through the Catholic Church abuse crisis and the Larry Nassar case, both of which showed highly credentialed, procedure-heavy bureaucracies functioning as designed while protecting predators. The article further argues that bureaucracy itself exhausts healthy, empathic professionals while rewarding those with unusually high appetites for control and conflict endurance, creating a differential selection effect that concentrates manipulative individuals in positions of power over time. The solution Chance proposes is a shift from rule-compliance to outcome orientation: leaders and boards must ask whether the organization is actually achieving mission, not just executing process.
points: * Rule-heavy systems create cover rather than constraint for sophisticated manipulators: if a box was checked, a meeting was held, a committee approved something, or a policy was technically followed, the predator claims integrity has been preserved -- and institutions tend to accept that claim. * Gerhard Blickle's research on the Dark Triad found that Machiavellian individuals with strong political skill are often rated favorably by coworkers and supervisors even while engaging in self-serving or harmful conduct; skillful manipulation looks like professionalism to people who aren't as slick. * Bureaucracy differentially exhausts healthy professionals while rewarding those with high appetites for control: empathic people assume good faith and tire of procedural warfare; manipulative individuals are energized by it, systematically outlasting the ethical staff who leave. * The Catholic Church and Larry Nassar cases both show highly regulated systems functioning exactly as designed while protecting predators: internal review processes, personnel procedures, and hierarchical reporting structures all operated correctly while the vulnerable were harmed. * The structural fix is to reorient boards, executives, and culture from procedure-compliance to outcome measurement: leaders must ask not 'did we follow the process?' but 'is this organization achieving its actual mission, and are the people in it being protected?'
quotes: Most people assume that more rules create safer organizations. Often, the opposite is true. Some of the most psychologically unsafe, ethically compromised, and structurally abusive environments are not chaotic organizations with no governance at all. They are highly regulated systems overflowing with policies, procedures, bylaws, compliance protocols, reporting structures, and credentialing requirements.

From the predator's point of view, if a box was checked, a meeting was held, a committee approved something, or a policy was technically followed, integrity has been preserved -- they cannot be called out. Good people are often genuinely confused by this behavior, because they would never think to use the rules that way.

Research by organizational psychologist Gerhard Blickle and colleagues found that Machiavellian individuals with strong political skill are often rated favorably by coworkers and supervisors even while engaging in self-serving or harmful conduct. Skillful manipulation looks like professionalism to people who aren't as slick. Expertise in working the rules becomes protective cover.

In many dioceses, allegations were routed through internal review systems, personnel procedures, legal processes, and hierarchical reporting structures that appeared orderly on paper -- while those same systems prioritized institutional preservation over vulnerable individuals. As abusive priests were moved from one diocese to the next, the system was functioning as designed.

Highly procedural systems disproportionately reward individuals with unusually high appetites for control, conflict endurance, and strategic manipulation. Healthy, empathic professionals generally enter organizations to build, solve problems, and contribute meaningfully. They typically assume others are operating in good faith. Manipulative individuals operate differently.

The same pattern appeared in the Larry Nassar case. Athletes, parents, trainers, and medical professionals raised concerns repeatedly. Within a highly credentialed sports and medical bureaucracy, those complaints were minimized, redirected, or procedurally managed. The institutional structure protected the abuser.

Leaders look like they are playing favorites when they hold some team members' feet to the fire while letting others spin out of control. This undermines the team, the culture, and overall performance.
